meta.title: Who really said "Effort only fully releases its reward after a person refuses to quit"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not in Think and Grow Rich. This sentence is a modern paraphrase of a line Napoleon Hill did write in chapter nine — here is the original wording.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Effort only fully releases its reward after a person refuses to quit'?
meta.ogDescription: Hill's books do not contain this sentence. It is a tidied-up paraphrase of a Broadway passage in Think and Grow Rich (1937). The real line, sourced.

answer.label: Not Napoleon Hill’s wording — a modern paraphrase
answer.authorDates: 1883–1970 · American self-help author · Think and Grow Rich (1937)
answer.sourceLine: The thought is Hill’s; the sentence is not. The wording appears in none of the Hill books we were able to search in full — Think and Grow Rich (1937), the sixteen Law of Success lessons, The Magic Ladder to Success (1930) and Outwitting the Devil — and no site carrying it names a book, chapter or page. What Hill did write, in the persistence chapter of Think and Grow Rich, is that Broadway pays off “only after one has refused to QUIT.”

source.excerpt: But Broadway is not easily nor quickly conquered. She acknowledges talent, recognizes genius, pays off in money, only after one has refused to QUIT.
trail: The sentence does not appear anywhere in the complete text of Think and Grow Rich, the book it is most often filed under — we downloaded and searched the whole book at the Internet Archive ↗, where the nearest match is the chapter-nine Broadway passage above.
It is likewise absent from the full text of Hill’s sixteen Law of Success lessons ↗, from The Magic Ladder to Success (1930) ↗, and from Outwitting the Devil ↗.
Wikiquote’s Napoleon Hill page ↗ does not carry the line in any section, and Quote Investigator has never written it up ↗, so there is no specialist finding to defer to here.
Every page that does carry it is a quote aggregator with nothing behind it: Goodreads ↗ and Quotes.net ↗ both list it under Hill’s name with no book, chapter or year.
source.excerptNote: This is the closest sentence in Hill’s book to the line that circulates under his name — and it is plainly not the same sentence. The capitals are Hill’s own.

author.name: Napoleon Hill
author.heading: Who was Napoleon Hill?
author.metaLine: 1883–1970 · American self-help author · Think and Grow Rich (1937)
author.bio: Born in Pound, Virginia in 1883, Napoleon Hill built a career as a journalist, salesman and lecturer before Think and Grow Rich (1937) turned him into the founding voice of American success literature. He is also one of the genre’s most unreliable narrators: Wikipedia’s biography describes him as a “self-help author and con man,” and notes that his claimed collaboration with Andrew Carnegie — the origin story of his whole system — has remained unsupported by any evidence. He founded the Napoleon Hill Foundation in 1963 and died in 1970.

misattribution.heading: What went wrong here
misattribution.intro: This is not a fake in spirit — it is a tidied-up restatement of something Hill genuinely argued. What is fabricated is the sentence itself, and the confidence with which it is served up as a direct quotation.

items.why: Hill’s sentence in the persistence chapter of Think and Grow Rich is a concrete image in his period register: Broadway pays off “only after one has refused to QUIT.” The circulating version drops Broadway, drops the capitals, and swaps Hill’s “one” for the modern, gender-neutral “a person” — a construction that reads as later editing rather than 1937 prose. Full text of the book ↗

Listicles routinely file the line under Think and Grow Rich, but the book’s full text does not contain it, and not one aggregator carrying it names a chapter or a page. Goodreads lists it with no source at all ↗

The line is missing from every section of Wikiquote’s sourced Hill page ↗, which does carry material from both The Law of Success and Think and Grow Rich, and Quote Investigator has never investigated it ↗.
The wording was already circulating in its present sourceless form on AZQuotes in May 2015, filed under “Inspirational, Effort, Quitting” with no book attached. Archived 14 May 2015 ↗

misattribution.truthLine: The idea is Hill’s; the sentence is somebody else’s. What he actually wrote, in chapter nine of Think and Grow Rich ↗, is that Broadway acknowledges talent and pays off only after one has refused to quit.

context.heading: What Hill was actually writing about
lead: Chapter nine of Think and Grow Rich is titled “Persistence: the Sustained Effort Necessary to Induce Faith,” and its argument is that persistence is not a virtue you are rewarded for having but a toll gate you pay before anything else happens. Hill sets the point in a specific place: he writes that he is looking up from his desk at Broadway, which he calls the “Graveyard of Dead Hopes” and the “Front Porch of Opportunity,” and observes that it hands out money and recognition only to people who have already refused to walk away.

His illustration is the novelist Fannie Hurst, who Hill says came to New York in 1915 to convert writing into riches and spent four years at it before the conversion came. That is the shape of the idea the internet later flattened into a maxim: effort does not pay in instalments, it pays after the decision not to quit has already been made.
context.detailsSummary: Why Hill quotes drift so badly
detailsBody: Hill is unusually easy to paraphrase into something quotable, because his prose is full of capitalised abstractions — PERSISTENCE, DESIRE, FAITH — wrapped in period imagery that dates quickly. Strip the Broadway scene out and you are left with a bare proposition, and a bare proposition is one edit away from a new sentence.

There is a second reason. Hill’s own factual record is poor: historians dispute his claimed work with Andrew Carnegie, Woodrow Wilson and Franklin Roosevelt. A body of work that already carries invented biography attracts invented quotation, because nobody carrying the line feels obliged to check it against a page.
context.pull: Hill wrote about Broadway. The internet rewrote it as a maxim about ‘a person’.

sourcesVerified.claim: The complete text of Think and Grow Rich contains, in chapter 9 ("Persistence: the Sustained Effort Necessary to Induce Faith"), the sentences "But Broadway is not easily nor quickly conquered. She acknowledges talent, recognizes genius, pays off in money, only after one has refused to QUIT." — and contains no occurrence of "releases its reward", "fully releases" or "refuses to quit".
The full OCR text of Hill's sixteen Law of Success lessons contains no occurrence of "releases its reward", "fully releases" or "refuses to quit".
The full text of The Magic Ladder to Success (Napoleon Hill, 1930, International Success Society) contains no occurrence of "releases its reward", "fully releases" or "refuses to quit".
The full text of Outwitting the Devil contains no occurrence of "releases its reward", "fully releases" or "refuses to quit".

Wikiquote's Napoleon Hill page, which has sections for The Law of Success (1928) and Think and Grow Rich, does not contain the sentence "Effort only fully releases its reward after a person refuses to quit" or any variant mentioning "refuses to quit".
A Quote Investigator site search for "refuses to quit" returns no article about this quotation or about Napoleon Hill and persistence.
Goodreads lists "Effort only fully releases its reward after a person refuses to quit." attributed to Napoleon Hill with 39 likes and no book or source given.
Quotes.net lists the sentence under Napoleon Hill's name with no book, year or source cited.

An Internet Archive capture dated 14 May 2015 shows AZQuotes already carrying "Effort only fully releases its reward after a person refuses to quit." attributed to Napoleon Hill, filed under the topics Inspirational, Effort and Quitting, with no source cited.
Think and Grow Rich was first published in 1937 by The Ralston Society.

Napoleon Hill was born 26 October 1883 in Pound, Virginia and died 8 November 1970; Wikipedia describes him as "an American self-help author and con man", states that his collaboration with Andrew Carnegie "has remained unsupported by any evidence", and records that he established the Napoleon Hill Foundation in 1963.
